title: Ecological economics

definition.text: A field of research, drawing on many disciplines, that studies how human economies and natural ecosystems depend on each other and change together over time and space.

facts.text: It treats the economy as a subsystem of Earth's larger ecosystem and stresses keeping natural capital intact, which sets it apart from mainstream environmental economics.
Ecological economists favour strong sustainability and reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital.
A main aim is to ground economic thinking in physical reality, especially the laws of thermodynamics and knowledge of living systems.
Besides efficient allocation, it puts weight on two further problems: fair distribution, and the size of the economy relative to the ecosystems it relies on.
Where mainstream economists tend to be technological optimists, ecological economists lean towards scepticism and favour precaution, since destroying key environmental resources may be irreversible.
Its topics include weak versus strong sustainability, energy economics and energy accounting, environmental services, cost shifting, modelling and monetary policy.
Economist Malte Faber describes the field as defined by its focus on nature, justice and time.
It was founded as a modern discipline in the 1980s through the work of European and American academics.

notes: Wants the flow diagram replacing the circular flow of income (S:53a741358ee6).

title: Costanza's valuation of the global ecosystem

definition.text: A 1997 study led by Robert Costanza that tried to put a total money value on the services the world's ecosystems provide.

facts.text: Published in Nature, it arrived at $33 trillion, with a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion, when total global GDP in 1997 was $27 trillion.
Half of the value came from nutrient cycling; estuaries, swamps and floodplains, and seagrass and algae beds had the highest values per hectare.
It averaged values from studies done in very specific settings and transferred them without regard to that setting.
Critics in the journal Ecological Economics still granted that valuing the global ecosystem had positive potential.

distinct_from: Source and sink functions of the environment

definition.text: The distinction ecological economics draws between growth, a quantitative rise in economic output, and development, a qualitative improvement in quality of life.

facts.text: Ecological economists argue that neoclassical economics confuses growth with development.
Beyond modest levels, higher consumption per person may not raise well-being and may harm the environment and society.
Growth of this harmful kind is sometimes called uneconomic growth.
Well-being in ecological economics is distinguished from the welfare concept used in mainstream and environmental economics.

title: Cost shifting

definition.text: The ecological-economics view that environmental and social harms are not occasional side effects ('externalities') but costs that businesses routinely shift onto others.

facts.text: Karl William Kapp's work explains why calling these harms 'externalities' is a misnomer: modern business makes profit by shifting costs onto others as normal practice.
Clive Spash notes that externality theory wrongly treats environmental and social problems as small exceptions in an otherwise efficient system.
On this view, internalising an odd externality does nothing about the structural problem.
Joan Martinez Alier points out that most affected consumers are future generations, who cannot influence today's prices.
By contrast, Paul Hawken argues that unsustainable goods are cheaper only because of a hidden subsidy paid by the environment, communities or future generations.

contested_note: Ecological economists dispute the mainstream view that harms can be corrected by internalising externalities.

title: Critique of ecosystem service valuation

definition.text: The argument, made by Douglas McCauley among others, that putting money values on nature and its services can harm conservation.

facts.text: Not all ecosystem services are financially beneficial: mangroves protect coasts, but wolves hunt cattle.

Money values tie conservation to fluctuating markets: bee pollination near a Costa Rican farm was valued at over US$60,000 a year until coffee prices fell and the fields were replanted with pineapple, which needs no bees.
Human ingenuity can replace ecosystem services by artificial means, which also lowers their value.
Conserving an ecosystem is not always more profitable than altering it, as local fish trade after the Nile perch was introduced to Lake Victoria shows.
McCauley concludes that campaigns should appeal to morality rather than money.

contested_note: Monetary valuation of nature is widely accepted among ecologists and conservationists, but some argue it is inherently false.

definition.text: How ecological economics grew from 19th-century and early 20th-century ideas into a discipline with its own society and journal by 1989.

facts.text: Its roots go back to the 19th-century Romantics, Malthus's worries about population and Mill's hope for a stationary state.
Frederick Soddy's 1926 book criticised the idea of the economy as a perpetual motion machine able to create infinite wealth.
Georgescu-Roegen's The Entropy Law and the Economic Process (1971) gave the field a framework based on material and energy flows.
The first organised meetings began in 1982 in Sweden; the field was formally founded in 1988 after a series of conferences.
In 1989 the International Society for Ecological Economics was founded and began publishing the journal Ecological Economics, with Robert Costanza as first president and editor.
The main founders were Herman Daly and Robert Costanza from the US, AnnMari Jansson from Sweden and Juan Martínez-Alier from Spain.

definition.text: The competing camps within ecological economics, from those close to mainstream resource economics to far more heterodox ones.

facts.text: Clive Spash sorts environmental work into three groups: new resource economists, new environmental pragmatists and radical social ecological economists.
Degrowth is a growing radical strand that addresses biophysical limits and global inequality.
Critics of degrowth among new resource economists point instead to the momentum of sustainable development and the green economy.

title: Non-western approaches to ecological economics
article: Ecological economics#Non-traditional approaches to ecological economics

definition.text: Cultural and traditional economic outlooks, such as Buen Vivir and Ecological Swaraj, that stress harmony with nature and are now counted as ecological economic practice.

facts.text: Buen Vivir ('Good Life') is a South American movement that rejects the western development model and does not value material accumulation.
Ecological Swaraj, from India, respects physical limits and non-human species and pursues equity through direct democracy.
Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful brought non-western ideas such as Buddhist economics into mainstream thought.

title: Green economy

definition.text: An economy that is low-carbon, efficient in its use of resources and socially inclusive; green economics is a more politically applied relative of ecological economics.

facts.text: The idea grew in policy circles first as a response to financial crisis and then as a vehicle for growth and development.
UNEP's definition was developed further in 2011 to stress a fair shift to a low-carbon, resource-efficient, socially inclusive economy.
It looks to cleaner, resource-saving technologies that cut emissions while addressing resource exhaustion.
It is closely related to ecological economics but has a more politically applied focus.

contested_note: Critics dispute whether market-based green economy policies can address the real causes of environmental crisis.

definition.text: The use of mathematical models to analyse how economies and ecosystems interact.

facts.text: Approaches include evolutionary, input-output, entropy and thermodynamic, multi-criteria and agent-based models, the environmental Kuznets curve and stock-flow consistent frameworks.
System dynamics and GIS are used for spatial simulation of changing landscapes.

definition.text: Ecological economics' work on money and monetary policy, aimed at sustainable scale, just distribution and efficient allocation.

facts.text: This work can be traced to Frederick Soddy's writing on money.
It asks whether interest-bearing debt forces growth, what money is, and whether alternatives such as alternative currencies and public banking would help.

definition.text: Tracking energy into and out of a system, the useful work done and the energy lost, to judge resource use and environmental impact.

facts.text: An energy balance uses the first and second laws of thermodynamics to show how much energy each point in a system needs and in what form.
A key idea is net energy gain: every energy source needs an initial energy investment, so its energy return must exceed one to be useful.
The net energy gain from coal, oil and gas has fallen over time as the easiest sources were depleted first.

definition.text: An economy with a constant stock of physical wealth (capital) and a constant population, so that it does not grow over time.

facts.text: Herman Daly's version keeps both stocks constant by a flow of natural resources through the system; that flow is the new ecological element added to the classical stationary state.
Both stocks should be as durable as possible: longer-lasting capital needs a smaller resource flow, and a durable population has long lives with low birth and death rates.
It rests on the view that the economy is an open subsystem of a finite, non-growing ecosystem, and must therefore itself stop growing at some point.
This contrasts with the mainstream picture of a closed circular flow between firms and households with no physical contact with nature.
Since the 1970s the idea has been linked mainly with Herman Daly.
It can apply to a city, region, country or the whole world.
Daly concedes that a steady state only postpones, not prevents, eventual exhaustion of minerals.
Sympathetic reviewers in the early 2010s judged it beyond what is politically feasible for now.

title: Stationary state in classical economics
article: Steady-state economy#Concept of the stationary state in classical economics

definition.text: The classical economists' idea that an economy would eventually stop growing and settle with a constant population and stock of capital.

facts.text: Classical economists contrasted scarce farmland with growing population and capital.
Capital accumulation would end once the rate of profit fell to a minimum or zero.
Adam Smith believed every national economy would sooner or later reach stationarity.
Unlike Smith and Ricardo, John Stuart Mill was optimistic about the stationary state, making what has been called a quality-of-life argument for it.

title: Daly's institutions for a steady state
article: Steady-state economy#Herman Daly's concept of a steady-state economy

definition.text: Herman Daly's proposal to create a steady-state economy by policy, through three state institutions limiting inequality, population and resource use.

facts.text: The first sets minimum and maximum incomes and a maximum on wealth.
The second issues transferable reproduction licences at the replacement fertility level.
The third sells depletion quotas that cap the flow of resources; unlike taxes, quotas directly minimise throughput.
Daly calls mainstream faith that prices and technology can overcome any scarcity 'growthmania'.

title: Solar-income budget
article: Steady-state economy#Herman Daly's concept of a steady-state economy

definition.text: Daly's term for the limit humans lived within before industrialisation, relying on the steady flow of sunlight rather than the stock of minerals.

facts.text: Daly sees two sources of wealth: a stock of minerals, which we can extract as fast as we choose, and a flow of solar energy beyond our control.
Because the Sun will keep shining for billions of years, the mineral stock is the crucial scarcity.
The Industrial Revolution broke the budget by extracting minerals at a rapidly increasing rate.

distinct_from: Daly's institutions for a steady state

title: Entropy pessimism

definition.text: The view that technology cannot escape the laws of physics, since every technology turns valuable resources into waste and so raises entropy.

facts.text: Neoclassical production functions treat technology as a factor of production with no mention of natural resource inputs.
In ecological economics, technology is the way natural resources are transformed in production.
Robert Solow replied in 1997 that 'elementary physics' had not by itself prevented growth in industrialised countries.

contested_note: Economists disagree on whether technology can overcome natural resource limits.

definition.text: Four works published between 1966 and 1972 on the importance of natural resources and the environment that led to ecological economics.

facts.text: Boulding's 1966 essay on Spaceship Earth argued that the economy must fit a closed, cyclical system.
Georgescu-Roegen's 1971 book argued that all natural resources are irreversibly degraded when used.
Howard T. Odum's 1971 Environment, Power and Society proposed the maximum power principle.
The Limits to Growth (1972) projected that output, food per person and population would peak and then decline.

title: Declining-state economy

definition.text: The argument, from Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen and degrowth thinkers, that a shrinking economy is better than a steady one for stretching finite minerals.

facts.text: Georgescu-Roegen argued Earth's carrying capacity will fall as finite minerals are extracted, so the world economy heads for collapse.
He proposed a 'minimal bioeconomic program' with restrictions stricter than Daly's.
Daly accepts a declining path but sees the steady state as the necessary first step: an economy must stop before it can reverse.
Rifkin, Latouche and Kerschner argue for declining-state strategies.

contested_note: Steady-state and degrowth advocates disagree whether the economy should stabilise or shrink.

title: Degrowth as a path to the steady state

definition.text: Christian Kerschner's view that rich countries should shrink their economies as a route to a fair world steady-state economy.

facts.text: Shrinking rich economies would leave ecological room for poorer countries to catch up.
Kerschner admits a world steady state may stay out of reach but says such goals can guide action.
Two comparative studies found no analytical difference between Daly's steady-state economics and European degrowth.

title: Capitalism without growth

definition.text: The question, raised by radical critics, of whether a steady or shrinking economy can be imposed on top of capitalism.

facts.text: Critics point to growth drives built into capitalism: the profit motive, jobs that depend on sales, credit creation by banks and labour-saving technology.
Governments need tax revenue from economic activity, and globalisation forces countries to compete.
Daly holds that the growth versus steady-state debate cuts across the left-right divide.

contested_note: Radical critics doubt a non-growing capitalism is possible; Daly argues the question cuts across left and right.

title: Resource decoupling
article: Steady-state economy#Resource decoupling and the rebound effect

definition.text: Economic activity becoming less demanding on nature, so fewer natural resources are needed per unit of output.

facts.text: It is measured by the ratio of total natural resource consumption to GDP.
Relative decoupling is a decline in resource use with all else equal; absolute decoupling is a decline in resource use while GDP keeps growing.
A 2019 review found that attempts to grow without environmental destruction had not succeeded.

title: Overdevelopment
article: Steady-state economy#The concept of Overdevelopment by Leopold Cohr

definition.text: The idea that rich countries of the global north are too developed, increasing humanity's ecological impact and causing problems for both rich and poor countries.

facts.text: It is based on Leopold Kohr's 1977 book The Overdeveloped Nations, mainly about overconsumption.

title: Space colonisation and limits to growth
article: Steady-state economy#Pushing some of the terrestrial limits into outer space

definition.text: The proposal that settling outer space could ease overpopulation and resource limits on Earth.

facts.text: In the 1970s Gerard K. O'Neill planned space settlements to solve overpopulation and limits to growth without political repression.

title: Great Stagnation critique of degrowth

definition.text: Wim Naudé's criticism that Western economies already resemble degrowth, in a 'Great Stagnation' of falling innovation and entrepreneurship.

facts.text: In prolonged stagnation, the economy increasingly works like a zero-sum system.

contested_note: Naudé's critique disputes the benefits claimed for degrowth and the steady state.

title: Ecologically unequal exchange

definition.text: The idea that world trade hides an unfair flow of materials, energy and environmental damage, not just labour, from poorer to richer countries.

facts.text: It describes an asymmetric flow of embodied materials and energy from peripheral countries, mostly in the Global South, to the developed core.
Southern countries serve as sources of raw materials, sinks for waste and sites of 'sacrifice zones', which deepens global inequality.
It builds on world-systems theory, which splits the world economy into a rich core and a poorer periphery with surplus flowing to the core.
Dorninger and colleagues found that half of all materials consumed by high-income countries are extracted from poorer countries, while rich countries gain trade surpluses.
A study of EU consumption from 1995 to 2019 found large parts of its environmental impacts outsourced abroad, while more than 80% of the economic benefits stayed in the EU.
Its logical result is that the Global North owes the South an ecological debt; unequal exchange is the mechanism and the debt its historical accumulation.
Jason Hickel proposes degrowth in the Global North to end these relations.
Peter Somerville criticised the theory as confused and internally inconsistent.

contested_note: Most cited studies support the theory, but critics such as Peter Somerville call it confused and inconsistent.
notes: Ecological debt is folded in here; it may have its own entry in the justice chapter.

definition.text: The flows of materials and energy between nature and society, between societies, and within them.

facts.text: These flows exist in every society, but their size and variety depend on culture, or the 'sociometabolic regime'.
They begin with humans taking materials and energy from nature, which are transformed, circulated, consumed and finally returned to nature as waste.
In-use stocks such as buildings, vehicles and infrastructure are built and maintained by these flows and provide shelter, transport and communication.
The concept extends the idea of metabolism from living bodies to the physical basis of society.
Each process's environmental impact depends on how it is done, the amounts involved, where it happens and nature's capacity to regenerate.
John Bellamy Foster built on Marx's ideas about social metabolism to develop the concept of metabolic rift.

title: Sociometabolic regimes
article: Social metabolism#Social metabolism as a proxy for human development

definition.text: Rolf Sieferle's classification of human history into hunter-gatherer, agrarian and industrial regimes according to their main energy source and conversion technology.

facts.text: Hunter-gatherers relied on 'passive solar energy' from recent photosynthesis, giving nomadic societies with low population density.
The Neolithic Revolution brought an agrarian regime of 'active solar energy use', with deforestation for farming, settled life and faster population growth.
The industrial regime relies on fossil fuels as its main energy source.
Indicators used to reconstruct this history include Total Primary Energy Supply and Human Appropriation of Net Primary Production (HANPP).

definition.text: The two main ways of measuring social metabolism: the Vienna school's Material and Energy Flow Analysis (MEFA) and the Barcelona school's MuSIASEM.

facts.text: Material flow accounting analyses a state's or region's inputs and outputs of materials and energy, including imports and exports.
MEFA, founded by Marina Fischer-Kowalski, studies national economies over time and standardises data for comparison.
MuSIASEM, built around Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi, studies subsectors of present economies with tailor-made accounts within a set 'grammar'.

definition.text: A school of heterodox economics, also called biophysical economics, that applies the laws of thermodynamics to economic theory.

facts.text: It studies how societies obtain and use energy and other resources to produce, distribute and consume goods while generating waste and environmental impacts.
Thermoeconomists hold that economies can be modelled as thermodynamic systems always involving matter, energy, entropy and information.
The global economy is treated as an open system, and economic activity as a dissipative system that thrives by consuming free energy.
It develops economic analogues of the first and second laws of thermodynamics.
A 2020 analysis concluded that GDP in advanced economies is likely to fall once credit can no longer prop up consumption and energy becomes lower in quality and more costly.

definition.text: Economic growth that reflects or causes a fall in quality of life.

facts.text: Herman Daly says it occurs when extra production costs more in resources and well-being than the goods made are worth.
The costs arise from the social and environmental sacrifices of a growing economy encroaching on the ecosystem.
David Suzuki argued in the 1990s that ecosystems can sustain only about 1.5–3% new growth per year, so demanding more from farms or forests eats into natural capital.
It is described as a pervasive ecological market failure: in a 'full-world economy' the ecological costs of growth may exceed its benefits.
The idea is usually credited to Daly, though some credit Marilyn Waring, who developed it in her study of the UN System of National Accounts.

title: Jevons paradox
article: Uneconomic growth#The role of technology, and Jevons paradox

definition.text: The proposition that technology which makes resource use more efficient tends to increase, not reduce, total use of that resource.

facts.text: Mainstream economists argue that growth from knowledge rather than more resources may not be uneconomic.
But knowledge-driven growth may still not solve the problem of scale: faster computers lead to more computers being bought.
Energy-saving bulbs lower household bills but free money for extra consumption elsewhere, an example of the rebound effect.
Efficiency lowers the effective cost of using the resource; if demand responds strongly to price, use rises enough to outweigh the saving.

contested_note: Economists debate how often the paradox occurs and how relevant it is to energy-efficiency policy.

title: Green logistics

definition.text: Efforts to measure and reduce the environmental impact of moving and storing goods, information and services.

facts.text: It began in the mid-1980s and aims to balance economic and environmental efficiency.
Packaging decisions set how many items fit per container and so strongly shape CO2 emissions per product transported.
Costs can be high: ammonia is 3-7 times more expensive than traditional marine fuels.

notes: Weakly connected to ecological economics; candidate to drop at selection.

definition.text: A spiritual and philosophical approach to economics that aims for the most well-being with the least use of resources.

facts.text: Its most basic feature is seeing people as interdependent with one another and with nature.
E. F. Schumacher coined the term in 1955 while advising Burma's government, and his essay was republished in Small Is Beautiful (1973).
Drawing on 'Right Livelihood', Schumacher held that work should develop a person's abilities, connect them with others and produce what is needed for a decent life.
Where traditional economics seeks profit and individual gain, Buddhist economics seeks to minimise suffering and to simplify desires.
It holds that non-renewable resources should be used only when most needed, and that relying on them means living on capital rather than income.
Traditional economics ignores 'primordial stakeholders' such as future generations and the natural world, who have no purchasing power.
Bhutan has promoted gross national happiness since 1972, based on Buddhist values, as an alternative to judging development by GDP.

definition.text: The physical law that in a system closed to matter flowing in or out, total mass stays constant: matter is neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged.

facts.text: In a chemical reaction, the mass of the starting materials equals the mass of the products.
Antoine Lavoisier confirmed it in the late 18th century, building on Jean Rey's 1630 demonstration.
Tracking how mass is distributed in a system over time is the engineering method called mass balance.
It holds only in the classical limit; Einstein's E=mc2 unified it with conservation of energy as mass–energy equivalence.
Hydrologists use it as a water balance to estimate how long water stays in a reservoir.

definition.text: The total energy needed to produce a good or service, counted as if it were stored inside the product.

facts.text: It aims to add up the energy of a product's whole life cycle, from raw material extraction and transport to manufacture, installation and disposal.
Because energy use usually brings greenhouse gas emissions, it helps judge whether a product adds to or reduces global warming.
A key use is comparing the energy a product produces or saves with the energy used to make it.
Common units are MJ/kg and tonnes of CO2; converting between them depends on the energy source used.
Values vary widely because there is no international agreement on data and methods, though products can still be ranked against each other.
Today's main methods grew out of Wassily Leontief's input-output model, adapted by Hannon to ecosystem energy flows.

definition.text: The ways databases estimate embodied energy: bottom-up process data, top-down input-output data, or a hybrid of both.

facts.text: Process data from manufacturers is more reliable and specific but usually leaves out much of a product's embodied energy.
Environmentally-extended input-output (EEIO) data from national statistics fills gaps but is much less reliable for a specific product.
Hybrid methods use process data and fill the gaps with EEIO data.

definition.text: The energy used to extract, process, transport, assemble, maintain and finally dispose of a building's materials.

facts.text: About 30% of all energy used over a building's lifetime can be embodied energy, depending on its age, climate and materials.
Its share has risen as efforts focused on cutting operational energy such as heating and cooling.
Rating schemes such as USA LEED include embodied energy when assessing a building's environmental impact.

definition.text: The energy used to make, maintain and recycle vehicles and to build transport networks, beyond the fuel burned.

facts.text: One French institute notes that people use more embodied energy in transport spending than direct energy.
France's ADEME puts a car's embodied energy at 20 800 kWh and an electric vehicle's at 34 700 kWh, the difference coming from the battery and electronics.
With a fuel EROEI of 8, fuel use should be raised by 14.3% to account for the fuel's own embodied energy.

title: Emergy

definition.text: The total energy of one kind, usually sunlight, used directly and indirectly to make a product or service; a way of expressing differences in energy quality.

facts.text: It puts sunlight, fuel, electricity and human services on a common basis by expressing each in the solar energy needed to produce them, measured in solar emjoules (seJ).
Howard T. Odum, studying energy flow in ecosystems from the 1950s, argued that different energy sources cannot be added without converting them to a common measure of quality.
Odum's first formal statement came in 1973; David Scienceman proposed the name 'emergy' in 1986.
Emergy accounting draws a system diagram, builds a table of resource, labour and energy flows, converts each to emergy and sums them.
Its stated goal is an 'ecocentric' valuation that adds information rather than replacing economic values.
Critics call it an energy theory of value, find unequal calories absurd, say the sunlight behind oil cannot be measured objectively, and fault it for ignoring market values.

contested_note: Emergy has been controversial in ecology, thermodynamics and economics, with critics rejecting its basic premises.

definition.text: The emergy needed per unit of available energy produced; a measure of an energy form's quality.

facts.text: If 10,000 solar emjoules are needed to make a joule of wood, the wood's solar transformity is 10,000 seJ/J.
The solar transformity of sunlight absorbed by the Earth is 1.0 by definition.
Odum's 1975 table of 'energy quality factors' first stated the energy hierarchy principle: quality is measured by the energy used in transformations.

definition.text: Ratios from emergy accounting that judge how a process uses local, renewable and purchased resources.

facts.text: The emergy yield ratio (EYR) measures how much an investment lets a process exploit local resources.
The environmental loading ratio (ELR) compares non-renewable and imported emergy with renewable emergy and indicates stress on ecosystems.
The emergy sustainability index (ESI) is EYR divided by ELR.

title: Energy return on investment

definition.text: The ratio of usable energy delivered by an energy source to the energy spent to obtain it.

facts.text: If EROI is one or less, the source becomes a net energy sink and can no longer serve as an energy source.
A fuel or energy source needs an EROI of at least 3:1 to be viable as a major source.
Charles A. S. Hall popularised energy analysis; his 1984 paper on the cover of Science gave EROI its greatest exposure.
Only human-applied energy counts as invested: sunlight driving biofuel crops is left out.
When EROI of an economy's main energy sources falls, energy gets harder to obtain and its relative price may rise.
For US fossil fuel discovery the ratio fell from about 1000:1 in 1919 to only 5:1 in the 2010s.
Researchers disagree on how far back into the supply chain to count energy inputs, so they reach different numbers for the same source.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on how to measure energy inputs, and an IEA-endorsed method gives more favourable values for solar panels.

title: EROI of energy sources
article: Energy return on investment#Application to various technologies

definition.text: Estimates of energy return on investment for particular technologies, from oil shale to hydropower.

facts.text: Hydropower plants average about 110 when run for about 100 years; nuclear plants range from 20 to 81.
Refined fuel from conventional oil ranges from around 18 to 43, while oil shale is typically around 1.4–1.5.
Wind turbines average around 16 unbuffered and 4 buffered in the literature; operating turbines averaged 19.8 in 2018 data.
A 2015 review found mean harmonised EROIs between 8.7 and 34.2 for photovoltaic modules, with payback times of 1.0 to 4.1 years.

notes: Figures come from differing studies and boundary choices; the verifier should keep each with its source.

title: Net energy and payback time
article: Energy return on investment#Relationship to net energy gain

definition.text: Net energy is the amount of energy gained from a source after subtracting what was invested, while EROI expresses the same thing as a ratio.

facts.text: A process with an EROI of 5 yields a net energy gain of 4 units for each unit spent.
Break-even is an EROI of 1, or net gain of 0; the time to reach it is the energy payback time.

definition.text: The argument that a declining energy return on investment helps explain why complex societies collapse.

facts.text: Thomas Homer-Dixon argues falling EROI was one reason the Western Roman Empire collapsed in the fifth century CE.
Joseph Tainter suggests a diminishing EROI is a chief cause of the collapse of complex societies.
Some historians link humanity's growing use of outside energy to easily exploited, high-EROI sources.

title: Expanded EROI calculations
article: Energy return on investment#Additional EROI calculations

definition.text: Three wider ways of counting EROI: point of use, extended and societal.

facts.text: Point-of-use EROI adds the cost of refining and transporting the fuel, which lowers the result.
Extended EROI also adds the infrastructure needed to transport the refined energy.
Societal EROI sums the EROIs of all fuels a nation uses; it has never been fully calculated.

definition.text: For a storage device, the ratio of electricity stored over its lifetime to the embodied electricity needed to build it.

facts.text: Reported values include 10 for a vanadium redox battery, 704 for pumped hydro and 792 for compressed-air storage.
A Stanford team found that without pumped storage, pairing wind with today's batteries would not be worth the investment.

title: Energy cannibalism
article: Energy return on investment#EROI under rapid growth

definition.text: The effect where rapid growth of an energy industry consumes the energy of existing plants to build new ones, limiting how fast it can grow.

facts.text: It limits the growth rate of energy technologies when climate neutrality is demanded.
A solar breeder, a panel factory powered by its own panels, overcomes some of these problems.

definition.text: A physical quantity often described as a measure of how spread out, or dispersed, energy is in a system; loosely, its degree of disorder.

facts.text: By the second law of thermodynamics, the entropy of an isolated system tends not to decrease.
Lower entropy marks more useful energy: energy supplied at a high temperature tends to be more useful than the same amount at a lower temperature.
Rudolf Clausius named the concept in 1865, from the Greek word for 'transformation'.
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen brought entropy into ecological economics, coining 'entropy pessimism', a position Herman Daly continued to promote.
Because of rising entropy, recovering materials dispersed as pollution and waste needs energy and resources that rise steeply as the recycled share grows.
Entropy is the only physical quantity that seems to give time a direction, sometimes called the arrow of time.

definition.text: The maximum useful work that can be obtained from a system as it comes into balance with its surroundings; often called 'available energy'.

facts.text: It depends on both the system and its environment, arising from the difference between them.
Energy in and out always balance by the first law, but in real processes part of the exergy input is always destroyed, as the second law requires.
Solar radiation provides most of the exergy for processes on Earth, including those that sustain life.
Exergy use has spread from engineering to industrial ecology, ecological economics and systems ecology.
Some systems ecologists see exergy as the natural world's analogue of economic currency.
Zoran Rant proposed the concept in 1956, extending work by Gibbs and Helmholtz.

definition.text: How much of a form of energy can be turned into useful work, measured as the ratio of its exergy to its energy.

facts.text: Electrical, kinetic and chemical energy are fully recoverable as work, so their exergy equals their energy.
Heat and radiation cannot be fully converted to work; the upper limit for heat is the Carnot efficiency, found by Sadi Carnot in 1824.
High-exergy energy carriers can do more kinds of work and so can be held to have more economic value.

definition.text: Proposals to use exergy analysis to make environmental policy fairer and more effective.

facts.text: Exergy analysis exposed a gap in national greenhouse gas balances, which often leave out emissions from international transport and so ignore import and export impacts.
Early cases suggest exergy-based taxation could reduce the tax burden on citizens.

definition.text: The work potential lost, or wasted, in a real process; also called irreversibility.

facts.text: Highly efficient systems destroy little exergy, and inefficient ones a lot.
The exergy destroyed in a cycle is the sum of that destroyed in each of its processes.

definition.text: The law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.

facts.text: In an isolated system, the total of all forms of energy stays constant.
It distinguishes two main ways energy moves into or out of a system: as heat and as work.
It has been precisely supported, and never violated, in many careful experiments.
Kenneth Boulding used the conservation of matter and energy to argue that the flow of resources through the economy roughly measures GNP, so GNP should be treated as a cost to minimise.

title: Heterodox economics

definition.text: A broad term for schools of economic thought that are not generally seen as part of mainstream economics.

facts.text: It is defined by contrast with whichever schools are most influential at a given time and place, so it has no fixed definition.
Schools usually counted as heterodox include the Austrian, ecological, Marxist-historical, post-Keynesian and modern monetary approaches.
Four frames of analysis are central to heterodox thought: history, natural systems, uncertainty and power.
It is an umbrella term rather than a single school, but its schools often see neoclassical economics as flawed.
Economist Marcos Lisboa argues that the assumptions critics attack are often not essential to neoclassical economics.
Frederic S. Lee estimated in 2007 that 5 to 10 percent of American economists were heterodox.
Student movements such as Rethinking Economics campaign for more pluralism, including heterodox approaches, in economics degrees.

contested_note: Heterodox schools reject parts of neoclassical economics, while mainstream defenders say the criticisms misread it.

title: Heterodox critique of homo economicus
article: Heterodox economics#Criticism of the neoclassical model of individual behavior

definition.text: The objection, shared by many heterodox schools, to the neoclassical picture of people as rational agents who maximise their own utility or profit.

facts.text: Rational, maximising behaviour underpins rational choice theory and is for many economists synonymous with economic behaviour.
Critics note that social constraints or coercion, or poor judgement of choices, may stop people from maximising pleasure.
Shiozawa argues agents in a complex world cannot reach maximum utility and instead pick from a repertoire of ready-made rules.

contested_note: Heterodox and neoclassical economists disagree over whether rational maximisation describes real behaviour.

title: Heterodox critique of market equilibrium
article: Heterodox economics#Criticism of the neoclassical model of market equilibrium

definition.text: The objection that neoclassical models of markets settling at efficient equilibrium prices rarely capture real markets.

facts.text: In microeconomic theory, many cost-minimising buyers and sellers imply market-clearing equilibrium prices, which are Pareto efficient under convexity assumptions.
Mainstream microeconomics is built on optimisation and equilibrium, while heterodox economics centres on institutions, history and social structure.

contested_note: Austrians, post-Keynesians and others dispute the realism of equilibrium models that mainstream economics relies on.

definition.text: The basic physical laws governing energy, heat, work, temperature and entropy, which rule out things such as perpetual motion machines.

facts.text: Thermodynamics traditionally recognises three laws, with a more basic 'zeroth law' defining thermal equilibrium and temperature added later.
The first law says energy cannot be created or destroyed; the second says the total entropy of interacting systems never decreases.
The first two laws rule out machines that make work without energy input, and machines that turn heat spontaneously into work.
The first and second laws were established by 1860 through Rudolf Clausius and William Thomson.
Ecological economics uses the first and second laws to build economic models that respect physical limits; by these laws a perpetual motion economy is impossible.

definition.text: The law that natural processes are irreversible: the total entropy of interacting systems never decreases, so heat never flows by itself from cold to hot.

facts.text: Its simplest form, the Clausius statement, is that heat does not spontaneously pass from a colder to a hotter body.
All natural processes are irreversible; reversible processes are only a theoretical limit.
It was first formulated by Sadi Carnot in 1824 in his study of the motive power of fire.
Georgescu-Roegen called it the 'entropy law' and made it central to his economics.

title: Metabolic rift

definition.text: A theory, credited by sociologist John Bellamy Foster to Karl Marx, that capitalism breaks the natural exchange of materials between society and nature, producing ecological crisis.

facts.text: Foster, not Marx, coined the term, starting with his book Marx's Ecology.
Marx wrote during England's 'second' agricultural revolution (1815–1880), when soil exhaustion pushed Britain to import bone and guano for fertiliser.
It drew on Justus von Liebig's 1840 explanation of how soil nutrients feed plant growth.
Nutrients sent to cities as food were not returned to the land as waste, a one-way 'robbing of the soil' that linked urban pollution with soil depletion.
Originally a critique of capitalist agriculture, it has been extended to marine ecology and to a 'carbon rift' from rising carbon dioxide emissions.
Foster sees in it evidence that Marx held an ecological outlook, against claims that Marx ignored nature.

contested_note: Historical materialists such as Jason W. Moore read the rift's origins and nature very differently from Foster.
distinct_from: Moore's reading of the metabolic rift

title: Moore's reading of the metabolic rift

definition.text: Jason W. Moore's view that metabolic rifts began with capitalism in the 'long' 16th century and recur in each phase of capitalist development.

facts.text: Moore holds that the split between social and natural systems is empirically false and arbitrary.
He traces the rift to capitalist relations based on the law of value rather than to industrial agriculture.
James O'Connor sees capitalist undervaluing of nature leading to economic crisis, the 'second contradiction of capitalism'.

contested_note: Moore's view diverges widely from Foster's on what causes ecological crisis.

title: Eco-urbanism and the metabolic rift

definition.text: Efforts in city planning to close loops by bringing a city's energy, water, food and waste flows back within its own systems.

facts.text: The aim is greater self-reliance through 'closed-loop systems' that reduce dependence on outside networks.
Critics link it to 'managerial environmentalism' and doubt sustainable cities are feasible within global capitalism.

distinct_from: Moore's reading of the metabolic rift

definition.text: Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism: an accounting method for analysing social-ecological systems and simulating possible development paths.

facts.text: It keeps assessments consistent across scales and across economic, demographic and energy dimensions measured in different units.
It tracks who uses which resources and why, the resulting environmental pressures, and how far needs and pressures are shifted abroad through trade.
Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi created it around 1997 at the Autonomous University of Barcelona.
It suits analysis of the nexus between food, energy, water and land use, and has been tested with the FAO.

title: Post-normal science

definition.text: A problem-solving approach for science used in policy when 'facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high and decisions urgent', developed by Silvio Funtowicz and Jerome Ravetz in the 1990s.

facts.text: In such cases it sets aside the traditional ideal of truth and focuses on quality, judged by internal and extended peer communities.
Its diagram plots system uncertainties against decision stakes, separating applied science, professional consultancy and post-normal science.
It complements risk analysis and cost-benefit analysis rather than replacing them.
It is meant to guide knowledge for decisions on pandemics, ecosystem collapse, biodiversity loss and sustainability transitions; ecosystem services are a topical subject for it.
In modelling it favours 'models to map our ignorance about the future' over models to predict and control it.
Critics say it adds no new epistemology, turns climate scientists into 'stealth advocates', and undermines empiricism.

contested_note: Critics argue it retraces older debates and weakens scientific neutrality and empiricism.

definition.text: In post-normal science, the wider group of stakeholders, beyond scientists, who share in checking the quality of scientific inputs to a decision.

facts.text: Participants are not treated as passive learners convinced by experts but resolve issues through debate and dialogue.
These spaces express differing values and power in a setting of inequality and conflict, so agreement is not guaranteed.
Some argue conservation science, with its many layers of policy-makers and stakeholders, has always been an extended peer community.

definition.text: Quantitative techniques linked to post-normal science: NUSAP for numbers, sensitivity auditing for indicators and models, quantitative storytelling and MuSIASEM.

facts.text: Post-normal science defines 'garbage in, garbage out' as when input uncertainties must be hidden lest model outputs become completely indeterminate.

definition.text: A worldview that sees Earth as a spaceship with limited supplies, whose passengers must act as one crew for the common good.

facts.text: The earliest known use is in Henry George's Progress and Poverty (1879).
Kenneth Boulding's 1966 essay contrasted the past 'cowboy economy' of seemingly endless resources with a future 'spaceman economy' with no unlimited reservoirs for extraction or pollution.
Boulding argued the economic system must fit itself to an ecological system with limited pools of resources.
Buckminster Fuller popularised the phrase in his 1968 Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth.
UN Secretary-General U Thant used it on Earth Day 1971, referring to the services Earth provides and our duty to protect it.
Sociologist Steffen Roth argues a realised Spaceship Earth would be the most total institution in human history.

definition.text: A family of non-equilibrium macroeconomic models built on strict accounting so that every flow and stock in an economy is included and adds up.

facts.text: They are popular in the post-Keynesian school and contrast with the DSGE models of mainstream macroeconomics.
Their accounting rule is that one party's asset is another's liability and no money comes from or vanishes into nowhere.
Wynne Godley used them to warn from 2000 that the US housing market would weaken and cause a recession.
They are now widely used in ecological macroeconomics, adding resource, energy and ecosystem stocks and flows, drawing on Georgescu-Roegen's flow-fund models.

title: Sustainability science

definition.text: An applied academic discipline, emerging in the 1980s, that studies sustainability and sustainable development and links knowledge to action.

facts.text: William C. Clark describes it as a field defined by the problems it addresses rather than the disciplines it uses.
It grew from publications such as the World Conservation Strategy (1980) and the Brundtland report Our Common Future (1987).
It was officially launched as an international field at a 2001 world congress in Amsterdam.
Recognising the epochal human impacts of the Anthropocene is at the core of much of the field.

notes: The page's 'Inter-disciplinary approaches' section contains vandalised sentences (S:9bfa6e7d3eb3, S:2e2d32d95aa1, S:16a5e45d0a47); do not cite them.

definition.text: A holistic, interdisciplinary branch of ecology that studies ecosystems as complex systems, applying general systems theory to ecology.

facts.text: Its central idea is that an ecosystem is a complex system with emergent properties.
It is especially concerned with how human interventions affect ecosystem functioning, and so includes economics in studying ecological-economic systems.
A central feature is applying the principles of energetics to all systems at every scale; Howard T. Odum was its most notable proponent.
Ecological work deals almost entirely with open systems, which exchange with their surroundings across their boundaries.
Ecological engineering combines systems ecology with engineering design.

title: Maximum power principle

definition.text: Howard T. Odum's principle that organisms, ecosystems and societies organise themselves to maximise their use of available energy for survival.

facts.text: Odum held that societies with access to higher-quality energy had an advantage in the evolutionary struggle.
In systems ecology the principle of maximum power efficiency takes central place; the most advantageous function occurs when the environmental load matches the system's internal resistance.

notes: No crawled page of its own; mentioned on Steady-state economy and Systems ecology.

definition.text: The quantitative study of how energy flows through ecological systems.

facts.text: It looks for the principles governing energy flow through the trophic levels of ecological networks.
Systems ecology treats these 'ecosystem laws' as formally analogous to the principles of energetics.

title: Unequal exchange

definition.text: The hidden transfer of labour and ecological value from poor countries, mainly in the Global South, to rich countries and corporations, mainly in the North, through structurally unequal trade.

facts.text: Because of biased terms of trade, poor countries must export much more labour and resources than they import to keep trade in monetary balance.
It rejects the Ricardian and neoclassical claim that free trade based on comparative advantage benefits all parties.
Arghiri Emmanuel and Samir Amin traced it mainly to wage differences between core and periphery.
Hickel and colleagues calculated the drain from the Global South from 1990 to 2015 as equivalent to 242 trillion in 2010 US dollars.
Northern power is maintained partly through patents: 97% of all patents are held by corporations in high-income countries.
A common critique is that wage gaps reflect higher productivity in the North; supporters reply that productivity is measured by prices.

contested_note: Critics attribute North–South wage gaps to productivity differences, which unequal exchange theorists dispute.

definition.text: Raúl Prebisch's finding that prices of raw materials exported by poorer countries fall over time relative to the manufactured goods they import.

facts.text: Prebisch identified the pattern for Latin American exports such as coffee and copper while working for the UN Economic Commission for Latin America.
His ideas laid the foundation for dependency theory and import substitution industrialisation.
A recent study estimated that unequal exchange may have reduced North–South convergence by 34% across 43 countries between 2000 and 2014.

title: Human Ecology, Human Economy

definition.text: A 1997 book edited by Mark Diesendorf and Clive Hamilton combining human ecology and ecological economics to sketch an ecologically sustainable future.

facts.text: It was reviewed in Ecological Economics and The Australian Journal of Agricultural and Resource Economics.

notes: A single book, not a concept; excluded.

definition.text: The flow of matter and energy that enters the economy from nature as resources and leaves it again as waste and pollution.

facts.text: In Daly's account, low-entropy resources are imported from nature, turned into goods, and the throughput is finally returned to the environment as high-entropy waste.
The simple circular flow of income ignores the linear throughput of matter and energy that keeps money, goods and services moving.
Daly's steady-state economy keeps stocks of capital and people constant with a minimal flow of natural resources, which he calls throughput.
Too large a throughput from human activity depletes geological capital and impairs nature's life-support services.
Degrowth mainly aims to cut the material throughput of affluent societies.
Any use of technology adds to cumulative matter-energy throughput, which limits purely technological fixes.

definition.text: The application of conservation of mass to the economy: tracking the mass of materials through a system so that everything that goes in is accounted for as product, stock or waste.

facts.text: Material flow analysis rests on two principles: a systems approach and mass balance.
Mass balance ensures waste and by-product flows are not overlooked, whereas economic input-output tables often leave them out because they lack economic value.
Allen Kneese, Robert Ayres and Ralph d'Arge set out a 'materials balance approach' to economics and the environment in 1970.
The principle came from Lavoisier's chemistry into chemical engineering and finally environmental science.

definition.text: The ecological-economics question of how large the economy should be relative to the ecosystems it depends on, alongside fair distribution and efficient allocation.

facts.text: In a 'full-world economy', the ecological costs of further growth may exceed its immediate social benefits.
Daly sees the steady state as a first step, after which society must decide whether the optimum is above or below present levels; he judges we have overshot it.
Daly concedes such optimum levels are difficult, probably impossible, to define.
Martínez Alier argues that as the economy grows, poor people lose access to environmental resources and bear a disproportionate share of pollution.

definition.text: An approach in ecological economics that studies change as mutual feedback and selection between social, environmental and economic systems.

facts.text: Ecological economics itself is defined as studying the interdependence and coevolution of economies and ecosystems.
The idea began in biology for two species evolving together and later grew into gene-culture coevolution.
Richard Norgaard brought it into ecological economics, showing how pests coevolved with pesticides and the institutions regulating them.
Norgaard and Giorgos Kallis applied it to water development, urbanisation and rural communities with their ecosystems.
